text: In T-SQL, writing a multi-statement stored procedure is simple: end each internal statement with a semicolon, and you're done. MySQL's command-line client, and a lot of GUI tools built on top of it, work differently. They use the semicolon to decide when to send a statement to the server. That's fine for one SELECT, but a stored procedure body legitimately needs semicolons inside it.

Here's exactly where that breaks. Create procedure, begin, declare x int, set x equals one, select x, end. The mysql command-line client sends everything up to that FIRST semicolon the moment it sees it — long before the procedure body is actually finished. It has no idea you meant all of this as one statement.

The fix is DELIMITER dollar-sign dollar-sign. This tells the CLIENT tool — not the server — to treat dollar-dollar as the new end-of-statement marker instead of semicolon. Now you can write DECLARE, SET, and SELECT inside the body, each ending in an ordinary semicolon exactly like normal, and only the very end of the whole CREATE PROCEDURE uses the temporary dollar-dollar marker. DELIMITER semicolon at the end switches the client back to normal.

This is the single most important thing to understand about DELIMITER: the MySQL server has no idea it exists. It's not SQL, it's not in the standard, and you'll never use it in application code — a Python, Java, or dot NET driver sends the whole procedure body as one string, with no command-line prompt around to get confused in the first place.

Once your procedure exists, you run it with CALL, not EXEC like T-SQL. Call GetActiveCustomers, parentheses. One more small syntax difference, easy to forget the first few times you switch between the two.

So: DELIMITER changes what the client waits for, not what the server understands, and CALL replaces EXEC. Next lesson, we look at MySQL's own specific functions and quirks — IFNULL, GROUP_CONCAT, and how lenient MySQL has historically been about type conversion. See you there.
